title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
This incident shows AI being used as a tool inside a social-engineering fraud, not a failure of a deployed AI product. Scammers used AI-generated text to produce personalized, convincing impersonation emails at a scale and quality that would have been harder to achieve manually. The failure point is not inside any one organization's system but in the broader availability of AI writing tools that lower the cost of targeted deception.

The impersonation worked by combining plausible detail about each target's work with a procedural veneer of legitimacy, delaying the payment request until trust was established. A human reader catching the fraud required noticing that a prominent host was personally handling logistics and that the sending address was a free consumer account, neither of which is a technical safeguard. No institutional check stopped the emails before they reached recipients.

What is not established is who operated the scam, which AI tools were used, or whether any confirmed financial losses beyond the described targeting have been verified through law enforcement findings rather than reporting.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other NPR staff members to defraud people seeking interviews on the popular radio show "Fresh Air." Authors, entertainers, and public figures have received highly personalized emails claiming to offer interview opportunities, complete with detailed references to their work and seemingly legitimate booking procedures. The scam eventually requests payment, typically $250 for production costs. A history professor at Misericordia University fell for the initial pitch but became suspicious when the email supposedly came directly from Gross herself and contained language that seemed AI-generated. She confirmed her suspicions when asked to pay money.

Cybersecurity experts note that artificial intelligence has made impersonation scams cheaper and more convincing than traditional versions. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from unofficial addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and a major radio host personally handling logistics. WHYY, NPR, and "Fresh Air" have stated they never charge guests for interviews and are working with law enforcement to investigate. Experts recommend verifying requests through legitimate organizational contacts rather than responding to suspicious emails, and they warn that such sophisticated AI-enabled scams targeting specific victims will likely become more common.
